title: How to Handle Holiday Flight Delays and Cancellations
summary: Prepare for Thanksgiving and Christmas flight delays with backup plans, rebooking steps, refund guidance, and CLEAR travel tools.
body_markdown:
Holiday flight delays and cancellations can affect more than an itinerary. They can mean missing Thanksgiving dinner, arriving after a Christmas gathering, or spending part of the holiday in an airport. You cannot control the weather or an airline schedule, but a flexible plan can give you more options when travel changes unexpectedly.


## **Why Holiday Flight Disruptions Can Be Harder**


Thanksgiving and Christmas bring more travelers into airports during a concentrated period. When flights are full, fewer seats may be available for rebooking. Winter weather can also affect several airports at once, creating delays that continue long after a storm moves passes.


The timing adds pressure. A two-hour delay may feel manageable on a regular trip, but during the holidays, it can mean missing a meal, family tradition, or connecting flight. Planning for that possibility before departure can make decisions easier if your itinerary changes.


## **Build Flexibility Into Your Holiday Itinerary**


### **Travel Before the Last Possible Day**


When an event can’t be rescheduled, build extra flexibility into your travel plans . Arriving the day before Thanksgiving or Christmas gives you more options than taking a flight scheduled just hours before the gathering.


This matters most when you have a connection, are traveling through a winter-weather hub, or need to reach a destination with limited daily service. If your first flight is delayed or canceled, a buffer day can help protect the rest of the trip.


### **Choose a Nonstop Flight When Practical**


A nonstop flight removes the risk of missing a connection and reduces the number of airports that can disrupt your trip. When a connection is necessary, choose one with enough time to move between gates and absorb a moderate delay.


Before booking, review the airport layout and check whether you’ll need to change terminals. A connection that meets the minimum requirements may still feel too tight when you are traveling with children, older relatives, several bags or, mobility equipment.


### **Consider the First Flight of the Day**


Early flights are generally less affected by delays that build as aircraft and crews move through the day. They may also offer more same-day rebooking options if plans change.


The earliest flight is not always the right choice. Make sure you can reach the airport with enough time for parking, bag drop, and airport security without creating a new risk of missing departure.


### **Know Your Backup Routes**


Before your trip, identify later flights to the same destination and consider nearby airports. A backup airport only helps if ground transportation is practical, so compare the full route before treating it as an alternative.


Save the airline’s contact information and know whether you booked directly or through a travel agency. The company that issued your ticket may determine who can make changes.


## **Pack for the Possibility of a Delay**


Keep medications, travel documents, chargers, a change of clothes, and essential toiletries in your carry-on. Add anything you would need during an unexpected overnight stay.


Do not place irreplaceable gifts, keys, or items needed for the holiday gathering in a checked bag. If the bag is delayed, those items may not arrive when you do.


Traveling with food requires another layer of planning. Confirm TSA rules before packing and keep perishable food at a safe temperature throughout the trip. If a long disruption would make the food unsafe, buy it at your destination instead.


## **Check Conditions Before Leaving Home**


Review your flight in the airline’s app and check the weather at your departure, connection, and arrival airports. A favorable forecast at home does not mean the aircraft or crew has avoided weather somewhere else.


Turn on airline notifications, but continue monitoring the flight yourself. Gate assignments, estimated departure times, and rebooking options can change quickly during a major disruption.


Do not assume a delay means you can leave home later. Airlines can revise departure estimates, and boarding may begin sooner than the latest delay suggests. Follow the airline’s instructions and remain prepared to arrive according to the updated schedule.


## **What to Do When Your Holiday Flight Is Delayed**


### **Confirm the New Departure Estimate**


Check the airline’s app, the airport departure board, and the gate display. Listen for announcements and confirm whether your gate has changed.


If you have a connection, compare the updated arrival time with the next flight’s boarding time, not only its departure time. Contact the airline as soon as your connection appears to be at risk.


### **Look for Rebooking Options Early**


Open the airline’s app or website while you wait to speak with an agent. Self-service tools may show alternatives before you reach the front of a customer-service line.


Compare the complete itinerary before accepting a change. A flight that leaves sooner may arrive later if it adds a connection or sends you to a different airport.


If you are traveling with other people, confirm that the new itinerary keeps the group together. Rebooking tools may split travelers across different flights when seats are limited.


### **Keep Records and Receipts**


Save delay and cancellation notices, new boarding passes, and messages from the airline. Keep receipts for meals, transportation, and lodging purchased because of the disruption.


Whether the airline covers those costs depends on the cause of the delay and its customer-service commitments. Keeping receipts makes it easier to submit a request when reimbursement is available.


## **What to Do When Your Holiday Flight Is Canceled**


### **Decide Whether You Still Want to Travel**


The airline may offer a later flight, a different connection, or a travel credit. Before accepting, consider whether the new itinerary still serves the purpose of your trip.


A replacement flight that arrives after the holiday gathering may not meet your needs. In that case, a refund may be more valuable than a rushed or significantly shortened trip.


### **Understand Your Refund Rights**


If an airline cancels your flight or makes a significant change, you are generally entitled to a refund if you choose not to travel or accept an alternative, such as a rebooked flight, travel credit, voucher, or other compensation. The refund applies regardless of why the airline canceled the flight.


Review the current[U.S. Department of Transportation refund guidance](https://www.transportation.gov/individuals/aviation-consumer-protection/refunds) before deciding what to do. Accepting a replacement flight or travel credit may affect your refund eligibility.


### **Check What the Airline Has Committed to Provide**


Meals, hotel accommodations, and ground transportation are not handled the same way by every airline or in every disruption. These benefits are often tied to delays or cancellations within the airline’s control, rather than weather or air traffic restrictions.


Use the[Department of Transportation’s Airline Cancellation and Delay Dashboard](https://www.transportation.gov/airconsumer/airline-cancellation-delay-dashboard) to compare each airline’s commitments. Confirm the cause of the disruption and ask the airline what it will provide before paying for an overnight stay.


### **Ask About Your Checked Bag**


If your new flight leaves much later or from another airport, ask where your checked bag will go. Do not assume it will automatically follow every itinerary change.


Keep the baggage tag and airline app information available. If the bag does not arrive, file a report before leaving the airport and save the reference number.


## **Planning for Thanksgiving Flight Disruptions**


Thanksgiving travel is concentrated around a few days, including the Tuesday and Wednesday before Thanksgiving and the Sunday after. During the 2025 holiday period—from Tuesday, November 25, through Tuesday, December. 2—Sunday, November 30, was the busiest day, with 3,134,613 screenings, about 26% more than the 2025 daily average.


If possible, avoid making the busiest return day your only option. Compare Friday, Saturday, Monday, and Tuesday flights as well as those on Sunday.


Thanksgiving dinner also creates a firm arrival target. If missing the meal would change the entire trip, travel earlier rather than relying on a same-day flight or a tight connection.


## **Planning for Christmas Flight Disruptions**


Christmas travel stretches across a longer period and often overlaps with winter weather. From Friday, December 19, through Wednesday, December 31, 2025, TSA recorded 34,639,304 screenings. Sunday, December 28, was the busiest day, with 2,924,593 screenings—about 18% more than the 2025 daily average. Christmas Day was quieter, with 2,066,118 screenings, about 17% below the average.


Review the forecast several days before departure and again before leaving home. If the airline issues a travel waiver, compare your options promptly. A waiver may allow you to change dates without the usual fee, but terms and eligible routes vary.


Christmas gifts can add complexity to a disrupted trip. Keep valuable or irreplaceable items in your carry-on when airline and TSA rules allow. Use gift bags or wait to wrap items until arrival in case airport security needs to inspect them.


Confirm holiday hours for airport transportation, rental cars and other services you expect to use after landing. A late arrival can become more difficult when local services close earlier than usual.


## **Traveling With Family During a Disruption**


Choose one person to monitor the itinerary and communicate changes to the group. Keep reservation numbers, medications, and essential items easy to access.


If relatives are traveling under separate reservations, the airline may not know that you’re part of the same group. Ask whether rebooking can keep everyone on the same itinerary, but be prepared to decide whether splitting across flights is acceptable.


Families traveling with children or older relatives should consider the group’s comfort and mobility needs before accepting a long overnight connection. The fastest available option may not be the most practical.

## **Keep Your Holiday Plans Flexible**


The best holiday disruption plan starts before you reach the airport. Build in extra time around important gatherings, choose an itinerary with recovery options, and keep essential items with you.


If a delay or cancellation occurs, check alternatives early, save records, and understand the difference between rebooking, airline-provided amenities, and a refund. A carefully considered backup plan can help you make decisions without losing sight of the reason for the trip.
